reflections: Where have I been digging “broken cisterns” lately?
What has God prepared me for that I haven't recognized yet?
What would it look like to go back to the “fountain” this week?

adults.title: Known, Called, and Shaped
adults.coverMessage: God knew me before I was born — His call and His living water are for me now.
adults.background: Jeremiah was called as a young man around 627 B.C., in the thirteenth year of King Josiah of Judah, and prophesied for some forty years. The northern kingdom of Israel had been carried away by Assyria a century earlier; now Assyria was collapsing and Babylon was rising. Despite Josiah's reforms, Judah kept turning to idols and to political alliances for security, and Jeremiah warned that not even the temple would save Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7). For this he was mocked, beaten, and put in the stocks (Jeremiah 20). Later in his ministry, Lehi also warned Jerusalem to repent (1 Nephi 1:4, 18–20).

cards.prompt: Think of someone who saw potential in you before you saw it in yourself. What difference did that make?
exampleAnswers: A teacher who pushed me to try something I'd never have attempted.
A leader who gave me a calling I didn't feel ready for.
A grandparent who always talked about who I'd become.
cards.facilitation: Let two or three people share. Jeremiah's story starts the same way: the Lord saw who he could be long before Jeremiah did.

verses.t: Then the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,
Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
Then said I, Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.
But the LORD said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak.
Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the LORD.
Then the LORD put forth his hand, and touched my mouth. And the LORD said unto me, Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth.
See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: Jeremiah was likely a young man when the call came, during the reign of King Josiah. The Lord's answer to his “I am a child” was not “you're older than you think” but “**I am with thee**.” Latter-day Saints understand verse 5 as a witness of **premortal life** and **foreordination** — that God knew and prepared His children before they were born.

cards.prompt: Jeremiah's first reaction was “I cannot speak.” What does the Lord's answer teach about how He views our limitations?
exampleAnswers: He doesn't deny the weakness — He promises His presence.
The call comes with the help to fulfill it.
Our sense of inadequacy isn't the final word on what we can do.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: When have you felt unqualified for something the Lord asked of you? What helped?
exampleAnswers: A new calling I didn't feel ready for. Prayer and a mentor's help got me through.
Becoming a parent. I learned to lean on the Lord one day at a time.
Being asked to speak or teach. Preparing and praying made the difference.

alternates.label: Option C · doctrinal
alternates.prompt: How does knowing you lived with God before this life change how you see your purpose here?
exampleAnswers: I'm not here by accident. I came with a purpose.
My worth was settled before I accomplished anything.
This life continues a relationship with God; it doesn't start one.

cards.facilitation: Give the class a moment with verse 8 before anyone answers. If someone shares a personal story, thank them simply before moving on.

backups.teaser: Personal: what has the Lord prepared you for?
backups.prompt: What might the Lord have “sanctified” you for that you haven't recognized yet?
exampleAnswers: A gift you take for granted.
A relationship only you can reach.
A trial that prepared you to help someone else.

verses.t: Hath a nation changed their gods, which are yet no gods? but my people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit.
Be astonished, O ye heavens, at this, and be horribly afraid, be ye very desolate, saith the LORD.
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: In ancient Judah, the best water came from a **spring** — “living,” always flowing. Without one, people cut a **cistern** into rock to catch rainwater. A cracked cistern leaked, so after all that labor you came back to an empty hole. Israel's “two evils” were leaving the spring _and_ trusting in something they had built themselves.

cards.prompt: What are the “cisterns” adults are tempted to dig today — things that take great effort but never hold?
exampleAnswers: Career achievement as the measure of worth.
Financial security as the source of peace.
Being busy as a substitute for being close to God.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: What helps you notice when you've drifted from the fountain to a cistern?
exampleAnswers: I feel restless or empty even when things look fine.
My prayers get shorter and more routine.
I reach for my phone or my work to fill every quiet moment.

alternates.label: Option C · deeper
alternates.prompt: Why might it feel easier to dig our own cistern than to come to the fountain?
exampleAnswers: Digging feels like control; coming to God takes trust.
A cistern shows quick, visible results.
Coming to the fountain means admitting we're thirsty.

cards.facilitation: Avoid turning this into a list of other people's mistakes. Invite reflection on our own habits — and share one of yours first.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Bring a paper cup with a small hole poked near the bottom and a tray to catch the water. Pour water in and let the class watch it drain. “A broken cistern looks like it should hold water — but no matter how much you pour in, it never stays full.”

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: We are not asked to manufacture our own peace. The Lord offers Himself as a **fountain** — a source that keeps flowing. Coming back to Him is less about effort and more about **returning to the spring**.

backups.teaser: A tree by the river: trust that holds through drought

verses.t: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.

For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.

backups.meaning: Jeremiah contrasts trust in human strength with trust in the Lord. Someone rooted in Him still feels the heat, but keeps bearing fruit because their water source doesn't dry up.

question.prompt: What helps your roots reach the river before the dry season comes?
exampleAnswers: Daily scripture study, even when it's short.
Prayer that's honest, not just routine.

backups.teaser: Jesus offers the living water Jeremiah described
backups.label: Cross-reference

verses.t: Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again:
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.

backups.meaning: Speaking with a Samaritan woman at a well, Jesus presents Himself as the source of living water. What He gives doesn't run out; it becomes a spring inside the person.

question.prompt: What's the difference between water you have to keep drawing and a well springing up inside you?
exampleAnswers: One depends on outside sources; the other becomes part of who you are.
With Him, peace isn't something I have to keep chasing.

verses.t: The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words.
Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels.
And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.
Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.

cards.heading: Notice
cards.body: When the vessel was “marred,” the potter didn't throw the clay away. He **made it again**. The clay stayed on the wheel and in his hands.

cards.prompt: What does it mean to stay “on the wheel” when life feels marred?
exampleAnswers: Keep coming to church and to the temple even when it's hard.
Accept correction instead of leaving.
Trust that God is still working on you.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: When has the Lord reshaped something in your life into something better than you planned?
exampleAnswers: A job loss that led to work I love more.
A plan that fell through and opened a better door.
A hard season that made our family stronger.

sections.title: Fire Shut Up in My Bones

verses.t: Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: Jeremiah tried to stay quiet, and couldn't. Testimony, once kindled, wants to be shared. Invite the class to notice this week where the Lord's word feels like **fire** in them — and to let it out.

youth.title: Where do you fill up?
youth.coverMessage: God knew me before I was born — and He is the fountain of living water.
youth.background: Jeremiah lived about 600 years before Christ in Judah, the small kingdom left after Assyria carried away the northern tribes of Israel. The Lord called him as a prophet while he was still young. The people kept turning to idols, and to powerful neighbors for protection, instead of to the Lord, while the Babylonian empire grew stronger to the north. Speaking the truth made Jeremiah unpopular; he was mocked and even locked in the stocks.

cards.prompt: What's something you were sure would satisfy you — that didn't?
exampleAnswers: A purchase you had to have.
Approval you kept chasing.
Finally getting the thing everyone else had.

alternates.label: Option B · lighter
alternates.prompt: What's the most disappointing “upgrade” you've ever gotten?
exampleAnswers: A new phone that was basically the same as the old one.
A sequel that wasn't as good as the first movie.
Shoes that looked great online and hurt in real life.

backups.teaser: Warm-up: real thirst, and what satisfies it
backups.prompt: Have you ever been truly thirsty? What did it take to satisfy it?
exampleAnswers: After a long game or hike.
Only water worked — not soda.

verses.t: Hath a nation changed their gods, which are yet no gods? but my people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit.
Be astonished, O ye heavens, at this, and be horribly afraid, be ye very desolate, saith the LORD.
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: The best water came from a **spring** — living, always flowing. With no spring you dug a **cistern**: a rock-cut pit for rainwater. A cracked one leaked, so you came back thirsty to an empty hole.

cards.prompt: What are the “broken cisterns” people run to today instead of God?
exampleAnswers: Likes and followers.
Stuff and status.
Numbing out — looks satisfying but leaks.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: When has something you were sure would make you happy left you empty afterward?
exampleAnswers: Winning a game. The high wore off fast.
Getting the thing I saved up for, then wanting the next thing.
Fitting in by acting like someone I'm not.

alternates.label: Option C · deeper
alternates.prompt: Why do we keep going back to “leaky” things even after they let us down?
exampleAnswers: They're easy and right in front of us.
Habit. It's what we already know.
They feel good for a moment, and we hope this time will be different.

cards.facilitation: **If the class is quiet —** name one yourself first: “I'll go — I thought a bigger calling would finally make me feel like enough.” Then wait out the silence; don't rescue it.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Bring a paper cup with a small hole poked near the bottom. Pour water in and let the class watch it drain onto a tray. “A broken cistern looks like it should hold water — but no matter how much you pour in, it never stays full.”

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: Everyone's thirsty for something. The question is **where you go to fill it** — the Source that never runs dry, or your own cracked cisterns that always leak.

backups.teaser: Jesus says He is the living water
backups.label: Cross-reference

verses.t: Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again:
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.

backups.meaning: Jesus told a woman at a well that ordinary water only satisfies for a while, but what He offers keeps flowing from the inside.

question.prompt: What's something that satisfies you for a while but always leaves you wanting more?
exampleAnswers: Getting new stuff.
Likes on a post.

backups.teaser: Walking away from the fountain, and what it costs

verses.t: O LORD, the hope of Israel, all that forsake thee shall be ashamed, and they that depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living waters.

backups.meaning: Jeremiah calls the Lord “the fountain of living waters” again and warns that turning away from Him means leaving the only source that lasts.

question.prompt: Why would anyone walk away from a fountain to dig their own water?
exampleAnswers: They forget the fountain is still there.
They want to be in control of their own water.

verses.t: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
Then said I, Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.
But the LORD said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak.
Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the LORD.

cards.prompt: Jeremiah said, “I am a child.” When do you feel too young for what God might ask of you?
exampleAnswers: Sharing what I believe with friends.
Leading in my quorum or class.
Making a big decision on my own.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: What would you do differently this week if you really believed God knew you before you were born?
exampleAnswers: Pray like I'm talking to someone who actually knows me.
Worry less about what other people think of me.
Try something hard I've been avoiding, trusting He'll help.

cards.facilitation: Youth often answer with jokes first. Smile, then ask the question again more quietly.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: God didn't tell Jeremiah he was old enough. He said, “**I am with thee**.” You don't need to feel ready — you need to know Who's going with you.

verses.t: Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels.
And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.
Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.

cards.prompt: The potter didn't throw away the marred clay. What does that tell you about how God sees your mistakes?
exampleAnswers: He'd rather remake me than replace me.
Mistakes aren't the end of the story.

primary.title: God Knows Me
primary.coverMessage: Heavenly Father knew me before I was born, and He loves me.
primary.background: Jeremiah was a prophet in Jerusalem about 600 years before Jesus was born. He was young when the Lord called him, and he felt too young to speak. Many people in his day had stopped following Heavenly Father, but Jeremiah kept teaching them, even when it was hard.

cards.title: I Am a Child of God

cards.body: Long ago, God called a young man named **Jeremiah** to be His prophet. Jeremiah felt too young! But God told him something wonderful: _“Before you were born, I already knew you.”_ God knew Jeremiah — and God knows you, too.

cards.title: Before you were born
steps: Have each child show a baby picture, or draw themselves as a tiny baby.
Ask: “Who knew you and loved you before you could even talk?”
Teach: God knew each of us before we were born — and He has special work for us to do.

cards.title: God knew me
cards.scene: A smiling child surrounded by soft rays of light, with young Jeremiah kneeling nearby looking up to heaven; no text.

cards.body: Share, simply, that Heavenly Father knows and loves each child by name.

backups.teaser: Hands-on: reshape play dough like a potter
backups.title: The potter and the clay
steps: Give each child a small ball of play dough.
Have them make a shape, then squish it and make something new.
Teach: When we make mistakes, Heavenly Father helps us become something good again.

reflections: What do I now do because I love the Lord, not just because I'm supposed to?
Where in my life is the Lord asking me to “buy a field”: to act in hope before I see how things turn out?
How have I felt Him draw me with lovingkindness, and how could I respond this week?

adults.title: A Law Written in the Heart
adults.coverMessage: The Lord wants His law to live in me, not just around me — and nothing is too hard for Him.
adults.background: These chapters come from the last, darkest years of the kingdom of Judah. In the fifth year of King Jehoiakim, the king cut up and burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies (Jeremiah 36). Babylon, under Nebuchadnezzar, had already taken captives from Jerusalem in 597 B.C., and in about 588 B.C. its armies besieged the city. During the siege Jeremiah was imprisoned and at one point lowered into a muddy cistern (Jeremiah 38), yet he bought a field at Anathoth as a sign that the Lord would bring His people home (Jeremiah 32). Jerusalem and the temple fell in about 586 B.C., and many were carried into exile. Lamentations mourns that destruction, while Jeremiah 31–33 promise restoration and a new covenant.

cards.prompt: What's the difference between doing something because a rule says to and doing it because you want to?
exampleAnswers: A rule gets the minimum; wanting to gets your best.
When it's in your heart, you do it even when no one's watching.
Rules can feel heavy; wanting to feels free.
cards.facilitation: Draw on everyday examples from work, family or sports. This week moves from a law kept on scrolls to a law written in the heart.

verses.t: The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.

cards.prompt: These words came to a people about to lose nearly everything. Why might the Lord lead with His love before His instruction?
exampleAnswers: Love makes us willing to listen.
We obey better when we know we're wanted.
His love doesn't depend on how well things are going.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: When have you felt the Lord “draw” you with lovingkindness rather than push you?
exampleAnswers: A quiet prompting to come back after I'd drifted.
Someone reaching out right when I needed it.
Feeling forgiven before I felt I deserved it.

verses.t: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:

Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD:

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.

And they shall teach no more every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the LORD: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the LORD: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: The law given at Sinai was written on **tablets of stone**. Jeremiah looks ahead to a covenant written in the **heart** — obedience that comes from within because we truly _know_ the Lord. The New Testament sees this promise fulfilled through Jesus Christ.

cards.prompt: What's the difference between keeping a commandment because it's written down and keeping it because it's written in your heart?
exampleAnswers: One is about compliance; the other is about love.
A heart-law keeps working when nobody's watching.
It moves from “have to” to “want to.”

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: Which commandment has moved, for you, from the tablet to the heart? How did that happen?
exampleAnswers: Tithing. It started as duty and became gratitude.
The Sabbath. Over time it became rest I look forward to.
Forgiving others, after I felt how much I'd been forgiven.

alternates.label: Option C · deeper
alternates.prompt: Verse 34 ends with forgiveness. Why might forgiveness be the key to having God's law in our hearts?
exampleAnswers: Being forgiven turns obedience from fear into love.
A clean slate gives us room to change.
It's hard to love a law that only ever condemns us.

cards.facilitation: Let a few people answer before you add anything. If the conversation turns to judging others' obedience, gently bring it back to our own hearts.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: The Lord isn't satisfied with outward conformity. He wants to change who we are, so that His will becomes **our desire** — and He promises to remember our sins no more as we come to Him.

backups.teaser: Personal: moving God's word from head to heart
backups.prompt: What practices help God's word move from your head to your heart?
exampleAnswers: Pondering, not just reading.
Acting on a prompting quickly.
Partaking of the sacrament with intent.

backups.teaser: Mercies new every morning, written among ruins

verses.t: It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

backups.meaning: These verses sit in the middle of a poem mourning Jerusalem's destruction. Even there, the writer finds that the Lord's compassion hasn't run out and is renewed each day.

question.prompt: Why do you think the Lord's mercies are described as new every morning rather than given once?
exampleAnswers: Because we need them again every day.
Yesterday's mistakes don't use up today's mercy.

cards.heading: The setting
cards.body: Babylon's army was besieging Jerusalem and Jeremiah was confined in the court of the prison. Then the Lord told him to **buy a field** — land that was about to fall to the enemy. He paid, signed the deed, and had it sealed and stored for the future.

verses.t: Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days.
For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Bring a clay or glass jar and a folded sheet of paper labeled “Deed.” Seal the paper inside the jar as you tell the story. “Jeremiah put his hope in a jar — a promise he trusted the Lord would keep long after he was gone.”

cards.prompt: What would “buying a field” look like for us — acting in faith on a promise when things look hopeless?
exampleAnswers: Making temple covenants during a hard season.
Planning for a future the Lord has promised.
Serving while still grieving.

verses.t: Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee:
Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me?

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: Jeremiah declared, “There is nothing too hard for thee.” Then the Lord asked him the question back. Invite the class to bring their hardest thing to the Lord this week — and to answer His question for themselves.

backups.teaser: An invitation to call, with a promise to answer

verses.t: Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.

backups.meaning: The Lord spoke these words to Jeremiah while he was imprisoned during the siege. He invites Jeremiah to ask, and promises to show him things he couldn't yet see.

question.prompt: When has an answer to prayer shown you something you didn't know to ask for?
exampleAnswers: I prayed about one job and was led to a different one.
I asked for relief and was given understanding instead.

youth.title: What's written on your heart?
youth.coverMessage: God wants His goodness written in me — not just on a list of rules.
youth.background: This week's chapters take place during Jerusalem's worst crisis. The Babylonian army surrounded the city, food ran out, and King Zedekiah kept Jeremiah locked up for warning that Jerusalem would fall. At one point Jeremiah was lowered into a muddy pit. Right in the middle of that, the Lord had him buy a field, a promise that families would one day come home. The city did fall and many were taken captive to Babylon, but the Lord promised a new covenant written on their hearts.

cards.prompt: What's a song you know by heart without even trying? How did it get there?
exampleAnswers: I listened to it over and over.
It means something to me.
I sang it with people I love.
cards.facilitation: Keep this light and quick — it sets up the main question.

verses.t: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:

Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD:

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.

And they shall teach no more every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the LORD: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the LORD: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: The Ten Commandments were carved on **stone tablets**. Here the Lord promises something new: His law written **in hearts** — goodness that's part of who you are, not just rules you check off.

cards.prompt: What's the difference between doing the right thing because it's a rule and doing it because it's who you are?
exampleAnswers: Rules need someone checking; hearts don't.
One feels heavy, the other feels free.
You keep doing it even when it's hard.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: Is there something you used to do because you had to that you now do because you want to?
exampleAnswers: Going to church. Now I go to see friends and feel the Spirit.
Reading scriptures. It started as a goal and became a habit I like.
Helping at home without being asked.

alternates.label: Option C · deeper
alternates.prompt: How does God write His law in our hearts? What's our part?
exampleAnswers: Through the Holy Ghost, as we pray and study.
Our part is to keep trying and stay willing to change.
He changes us over time as we keep choosing Him.

cards.facilitation: If answers stay surface-level, share a real example from your own life first, then ask again.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Hold up a printed list of rules next to your phone playing a few seconds of a song the class knows. “Nobody needs to read the lyrics to that song — it's already inside you. That's what the Lord wants His goodness to be.”

backups.teaser: A fresh start every morning

verses.t: It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

backups.meaning: Written after Jerusalem was destroyed, these verses say God's mercy never runs out. Every day it starts fresh.

question.prompt: How could remembering this change a bad morning?
exampleAnswers: Yesterday doesn't have to decide today.
I can ask for help again without feeling like a bother.

sections.title: Buying a Field in a War Zone

cards.heading: The story
cards.body: An enemy army surrounded Jerusalem. Jeremiah was locked up. And the Lord told him to **buy a field** — land that was about to be taken. It looked foolish. It was a promise: _people will live and plant here again_.

verses.t: For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.

cards.prompt: What's a way you can “buy a field” — act on hope when things look bad?
exampleAnswers: Keep preparing for a mission or the temple.
Keep trying with a friend who's drifting.
Keep praying when it feels like nothing's happening.

verses.t: Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: The Lord's promise is simple: **call, and He will answer**. Invite the class to call on Him this week about one real thing — and watch for “great and mighty things” they didn't expect.

backups.teaser: Loved with a love that never ends

verses.t: The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.

backups.meaning: The Lord tells His scattered people that His love for them is everlasting, and that His kindness is what draws them back to Him.

question.prompt: What's the difference between being pushed toward God and being drawn by His love?
exampleAnswers: Being drawn feels like my choice, not pressure.
Love makes me want to come closer.

primary.title: God's Love Lasts Forever
primary.coverMessage: Heavenly Father loves me with a love that never ends.
primary.background: Jeremiah lived when an enemy army surrounded Jerusalem and many people were afraid. Even in that hard time, the Lord told Jeremiah that He loved His people with an everlasting love and would help them come home again (Jeremiah 31:3).

cards.body: The prophet **Jeremiah** lived at a scary time. An army was outside the city. But Heavenly Father gave Jeremiah a happy message for His people: _“I have loved thee with an everlasting love.”_ Everlasting means it never, ever stops.

cards.title: A heart full of love
steps: Give each child a paper heart.
Have them draw someone who loves them, or something Heavenly Father made for them.
Teach: Heavenly Father wants His love to be in our hearts all the time.

cards.title: Loved forever
cards.scene: Jeremiah sitting peacefully and writing on a scroll, with a large heart shape glowing in the sky above Jerusalem's walls; no text.

cards.body: Share, simply, that Heavenly Father's love for each child never ends — even when they make mistakes.

reflections: Like Daniel, who “purposed in his heart,” what do I need to decide before the pressure comes?
What would my faith look like if the Lord didn't answer my prayer the way I hope, “but if not”?
What daily habit of prayer or devotion would I want to keep even if it cost me something?

adults.title: Faithful in Babylon
adults.coverMessage: God can deliver me, and even if He doesn't deliver me the way I hope, I will still trust Him.
adults.background: Daniel opens in about 605 B.C., when Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon took the first captives from Jerusalem, including young men of noble families (Daniel 1:1–4). Daniel and his friends Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah were given Babylonian names (Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego) and trained to serve in the king's court. Chapters 1–6 tell how they stayed true to the Lord under Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar and Darius the Mede. Chapters 2 and 7 add prophetic visions of earthly kingdoms rising and falling until God sets up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.

cards.prompt: When have you been the only one in a group holding to a standard? What made it easier or harder?
exampleAnswers: At a work dinner where everyone else was drinking.
On a team trip when I was the only one who wanted to find a church.
It got easier once one other person stood with me.
cards.facilitation: Invite light, everyday examples. Daniel and his friends were young people far from home making exactly these kinds of choices.

verses.t: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.

cards.prompt: Daniel decided what he would do before the food was ever set in front of him. Why does deciding in advance make faithfulness easier?
exampleAnswers: In the moment, pressure and fatigue make it harder to think clearly.
A settled decision removes the daily negotiation with yourself.
It lets you answer kindly instead of defensively.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: What is a decision you made once that has protected you many times since?
exampleAnswers: Deciding never to look at certain content online.
Committing to pay tithing first, before other bills.
Choosing to attend church even when traveling.

cards.facilitation: Allow a moment of quiet after the question. If someone shares a personal standard, thank them without turning it into a rule for everyone.

backups.teaser: What God gave the four who stayed true

verses.t: As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.

backups.meaning: After Daniel and his friends kept their commitment about the king's food, God blessed them with knowledge, skill and wisdom. Their faithfulness came first; the gifts followed.

question.prompt: How have you seen the Lord add capacity after you chose to keep a commitment?
exampleAnswers: Keeping the Sabbath somehow left me more time, not less.
I found strength for a calling I didn't feel qualified for.

cards.heading: The setting
cards.body: Nebuchadnezzar raised a golden image on the plain of Dura and ordered every official to bow when the music played. Anyone who refused would be thrown into a **burning fiery furnace**. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were accused, and the angry king gave them one more chance.

verses.t: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, answered and said to the king, O Nebuchadnezzar, we are not careful to answer thee in this matter.
If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.

cards.prompt: They were sure God could deliver them, and still said “but if not.” What does that kind of faith look like in an ordinary life today?
exampleAnswers: Keeping covenants even when a prayer isn't answered the way we asked.
Trusting God's goodness without demanding a particular outcome.
Choosing what's right because it's right, not because it will be rewarded.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: When have you had to keep trusting the Lord after things didn't turn out the way you prayed for?
exampleAnswers: A loved one wasn't healed, and I had to decide whether God was still good.
A job or mission plan fell through, and I kept going anyway.
I prayed for a child to come back to church and I'm still waiting.

alternates.label: Option C · deeper
alternates.prompt: Why might a faith that depends on getting what we ask for be fragile?
exampleAnswers: It turns God into a vending machine instead of a Father.
The first disappointment can break it.
It's really faith in an outcome, not in Him.

cards.facilitation: This question can touch real grief. Let people share without trying to explain their trials away. A simple “thank you for trusting us with that” is enough.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: Faith is not a guarantee of a particular rescue. It is trust in **who God is**. The three Hebrews were delivered, and they also found someone walking with them in the fire.

backups.teaser: A fourth figure walking in the fire

verses.t: Then Nebuchadnezzar the king was astonied, and rose up in haste, and spake, and said unto his counsellors, Did not we cast three men bound into the midst of the fire? They answered and said unto the king, True, O king.
He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.

backups.meaning: The king sees the three men walking free in the furnace with a fourth companion. The Lord didn't keep them out of the fire; He was with them in it.

question.prompt: What does it mean to you that the Lord met them inside the fire instead of stopping it?
exampleAnswers: He doesn't always remove trials, but He doesn't leave us alone in them.
The only thing the fire took was what had bound them.

backups.teaser: Personal: the Lord with you in a trial
backups.prompt: The king saw a fourth person in the fire. How has the Lord been with you in a trial rather than taking it away?
exampleAnswers: I felt peace I couldn't explain during a hard diagnosis.
The right person called on exactly the right day.
I didn't feel alone, even though the problem stayed.

verses.t: Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Show a phone charger. Ask what happens to a phone that is only charged when the battery is almost dead. Daniel's prayers three times a day were his steady charge, so when the crisis came, he had strength already stored.

cards.prompt: Daniel prayed “as he did aforetime,” the same as always, even after the decree. What makes ordinary, daily devotion so powerful when a crisis comes?
exampleAnswers: The habit is already in place when we need it most.
We already know the way to the Lord, so we don't have to find it in a panic.
Small daily choices build trust that holds under pressure.
cards.facilitation: Some may feel guilty about inconsistent prayer. Keep the tone hopeful: the point is that starting a small, steady habit now matters.

backups.teaser: Daniel's own account of the night in the den

verses.t: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt.

backups.meaning: Daniel tells the king that God sent an angel to shut the lions' mouths. He credits the Lord for his safety and calmly states his innocence.

question.prompt: What do you notice about how Daniel speaks to the king who had him thrown to the lions?
exampleAnswers: He's respectful, not bitter.
He gives God the credit right away.

sections.title: A Kingdom That Shall Never Be Destroyed

verses.t: And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.

Forasmuch as thou sawest that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it brake in pieces the iron, the brass, the clay, the silver, and the gold; the great God hath made known to the king what shall come to pass hereafter: and the dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a great image of gold, silver, brass, iron and clay, broken by a **stone cut out without hands** that grew into a mountain filling the earth. Latter-day Saints have long understood the stone as the kingdom of God set up in the last days, which will grow until it fills the earth.

cards.prompt: Empires like Babylon looked permanent and fell. What gives you confidence that God's kingdom will last?
exampleAnswers: It's built by God, not by human power.
History shows that kingdoms of force don't last.
I've seen the gospel change lives, one person at a time.
cards.facilitation: Keep this short and hopeful. If time is tight, ask for just one or two answers and move to the closing.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: Daniel and his friends lived as faithful exiles in a powerful culture that didn't share their beliefs. The Lord asks the same of us: **purpose in our hearts**, pray as usual, and trust Him, even if not.

youth.title: Even if not
youth.coverMessage: I can stay true to God when it's hard, and trust Him even when things don't go my way.
youth.background: Daniel and three friends were teenagers or young men when Babylon's army took them from Jerusalem, about 600 years before Christ. In Babylon they got new names, new schools and a new menu, all meant to make them forget who they were. These chapters show how they stayed loyal to God in a culture that pushed hard the other way, even when the king threatened a fiery furnace and a den of lions.

cards.prompt: What's something everyone around you does that you've decided not to do?
exampleAnswers: Using certain language.
Watching shows I know make me feel worse.
Joining in when people make fun of someone.

alternates.label: Option B · lighter
alternates.prompt: If you moved to a new country tomorrow, what's one thing about you that you'd never want to change?
exampleAnswers: How I treat my family.
My sense of humor.
Going to church.

cards.facilitation: Answer first yourself with something real but light. Don't push anyone to share standards they feel shy about.

verses.t: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: The king's food likely included things the law of Moses forbade, or food offered to idols. Daniel didn't make a scene. He **asked politely** for a ten-day test, and the Lord blessed him and his friends with health and wisdom.

cards.prompt: Daniel “purposed in his heart” before anyone pressured him. Why is it easier to stand for something you've already decided?
exampleAnswers: You don't have to think about it on the spot.
People respect it more when you're calm about it.
It's harder to get talked out of something you're sure of.
cards.facilitation: If someone shares a time they gave in, thank them for being honest. The goal is hope for next time, not shame.

backups.teaser: What God gave Daniel and his friends

verses.t: As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.

backups.meaning: After Daniel and his friends chose to keep God's standards, God blessed them with knowledge and wisdom. Their choice came first; the blessing followed.

question.prompt: How might one small choice to obey open the door to bigger blessings?
exampleAnswers: It builds trust between me and God.
It makes the next right choice easier.

verses.t: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, answered and said to the king, O Nebuchadnezzar, we are not careful to answer thee in this matter.
If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.

cards.prompt: “But if not” means even if He doesn't save them. Why would they still choose God if He might not rescue them?
exampleAnswers: Because they loved Him, not just what He could do for them.
Because doing what's right was more important than staying safe.
Because they trusted Him even without knowing the ending.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: Have you ever prayed for something that didn't happen? How did you keep going?
exampleAnswers: I prayed to make a team and didn't, but I felt God still cared.
A friend moved away even though I prayed she wouldn't.
I'm still waiting, and talking to someone helped.

alternates.label: Option C · deeper
alternates.prompt: Is it still faith if you're scared? What does this story say?
exampleAnswers: Yes. Faith is doing it anyway, not feeling no fear.
They didn't say they weren't afraid. They said they wouldn't bow.
Courage and faith can show up together.

cards.facilitation: Leave real silence after the question. If a hard experience comes up, listen and thank them. You don't need to explain why prayers aren't always answered the way we want.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Hold up a seatbelt (or draw one). You don't buckle it because you expect a crash. You buckle it before you know what will happen. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego had already buckled in their faith before the furnace.

verses.t: He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: God didn't keep them out of the fire. He **walked with them in it**. He does the same for us in hard times, even when the problem doesn't disappear.

verses.t: Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.

cards.prompt: Praying could literally get Daniel thrown to lions, and he kept doing it. What's one small habit with God you could keep no matter what this week?
exampleAnswers: A short prayer every morning before my phone.
Reading one verse before bed.
Thanking God for one thing each day.
cards.facilitation: Invite them to think of an answer privately if they'd rather not say it out loud.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: Daniel and his friends lived in a world that didn't share their faith, and they stayed true without being rude or proud. You can too: **decide early, pray often, and trust God, even if not.**

backups.teaser: How Daniel explained surviving the lions

verses.t: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt.

backups.meaning: In the morning Daniel told the king that God had sent an angel to shut the lions' mouths. He gave the credit to God.

question.prompt: Why do you think Daniel gave God the credit instead of himself?
exampleAnswers: He knew he couldn't have survived on his own.
Being humble is part of being faithful.

primary.title: Daniel Was Brave
primary.coverMessage: I can choose the right and pray to Heavenly Father, even when it's hard.
primary.background: Daniel was a young man taken far from home to the land of Babylon. He kept praying to Heavenly Father every day, even when the king made a rule against it. Heavenly Father protected him in a den of lions (Daniel 6).

cards.body: **Daniel** loved Heavenly Father and prayed to Him three times every day. Some men who didn't like Daniel tricked the king into making a rule: no one could pray to God. Daniel prayed anyway, by his open window. So he was put in a den of hungry lions! But in the morning Daniel was safe. He told the king: _“My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths.”_ Daniel was brave because he kept praying.

cards.title: Brave like Daniel
steps: Have the children pretend to be lions: roar, then close their mouths tight when you say “the angel came!”
Ask: When can we pray? (Morning, night, when we're scared, when we're happy.)
Teach: We can be brave like Daniel by praying every day.

cards.title: Safe with the lions
cards.scene: Daniel kneeling calmly in prayer inside a den with sleepy, gentle lions resting around him and an angel's soft light above; no text.

cards.body: Share, simply, that Heavenly Father hears every child's prayers and helps them be brave.

reflections: Where have I been keeping my distance from the Lord because I assumed He was disappointed in me?
What would it look like for me this week to “rend your heart, and not your garments”?
How have I felt the Lord draw me back with “bands of love” after I wandered?

adults.title: Love That Buys Us Back
adults.coverMessage: The Lord's covenant love keeps reaching for me, and He will heal me when I turn back to Him.
adults.background: Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel in the 700s B.C., in the years before Assyria conquered it (Hosea 1:1). Israel was prosperous but had turned to Baal worship and to alliances with foreign powers. The Lord had Hosea marry Gomer, who was unfaithful, and later redeem her, so that his own family became a living picture of the Lord's love for an unfaithful people. Joel's date is uncertain. He describes a devastating plague of locusts as a call to repent before “the day of the Lord,” and he promises that the Lord will restore what was lost and pour out His Spirit.

cards.prompt: What does it take to keep loving someone who keeps letting you down?
exampleAnswers: Remembering who they really are underneath.
Patience, and a lot of prayer.
Deciding love is a commitment, not just a feeling.
cards.facilitation: This can touch tender family situations. Keep it general and don't ask for details. Hosea's story is about the Lord's love for people who wandered.

cards.heading: The setting
cards.body: Hosea's wife Gomer left him for other lovers. Instead of abandoning her, Hosea **paid to bring her home**. The Lord used Hosea's marriage to show Israel how He saw them: a covenant partner who had wandered, and whom He still wanted back.

verses.t: Then said the LORD unto me, Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine.
And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies.
I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the LORD.

cards.prompt: Why do you think the Lord chose a marriage, with all its hurt and loyalty, to describe His relationship with His people?
exampleAnswers: A covenant is personal, not just a set of rules.
Betrayal hurts most where love runs deepest.
It shows He is committed to us even when we aren't to Him.

alternates.label: Option B · deeper
alternates.prompt: Hosea had to pay a price to bring Gomer back. How does that point to the Savior?
exampleAnswers: Christ paid the price to redeem us from what we'd sold ourselves into.
Redemption costs the redeemer, not the redeemed.
He came after us; we didn't earn our way back.

cards.facilitation: Marriage and betrayal can be tender topics. Keep the focus on the Lord's faithfulness rather than inviting stories about anyone's marriage.

backups.teaser: Drawn with bands of love, not force

verses.t: I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws, and I laid meat unto them.

backups.meaning: The Lord describes leading Israel the way a kind farmer eases the yoke and feeds his animals. He draws His people with love, not force.

question.prompt: What are the cords of love that have drawn you back to the Lord?
exampleAnswers: A friend who kept inviting me without judging.
Tender mercies I couldn't explain away.

verses.t: O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity.
Take with you words, and turn to the LORD: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips.
Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods: for in thee the fatherless findeth mercy.
I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.

cards.prompt: The Lord says, “I will love them freely.” What keeps people from believing His love is really free and not earned?
exampleAnswers: We know our own mistakes too well.
We're used to love that has conditions.
We confuse His love with His approval of everything we do.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: When have you felt the Lord welcome you back after you'd drifted?
exampleAnswers: Coming back to church after years away and being greeted warmly.
A prayer after a long silence that felt answered right away.
Taking the sacrament again after repenting.

cards.facilitation: Some in the room may feel they've drifted too far. Let the words “I will love them freely” rest for a moment before moving on.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: The invitation is simple: **“Take with you words, and turn to the Lord.”** He doesn't wait for us to fix ourselves first. He promises to heal the very wandering we bring to Him.

backups.teaser: Returning together to the One who heals

verses.t: Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up.

backups.meaning: Hosea pictures the people encouraging each other to return to the Lord, trusting that the One who allowed the hard consequences will also heal and bind them up.

question.prompt: Why might returning together be easier than returning alone?
exampleAnswers: Others remind us we're not the only ones who strayed.
Shared hope makes it feel possible.

backups.teaser: Personal: the bands of love in your life
backups.prompt: Hosea 11:4 says the Lord draws us “with bands of love.” What are some of those bands in your life?
exampleAnswers: A friend who kept inviting me.
Scriptures that seemed written for me at the right time.
Answered prayers I didn't expect.

verses.t: Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning:
And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Show a beautifully wrapped box that is empty and a plain paper bag with a real gift inside. Tearing clothing was an outward sign of sorrow. The Lord asks for what's inside: a changed heart, not just the wrapping.

cards.prompt: What's the difference between showing repentance and actually having a changed heart?
exampleAnswers: One is for others to see; the other is between me and God.
Outward signs can stop at feeling bad; real change keeps going.
A changed heart shows up in what I do next week.
cards.facilitation: Avoid making this about judging others' sincerity. Point the question toward our own hearts.

backups.teaser: Restoring the years the locusts ate

verses.t: And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.

backups.meaning: After a devastating plague, the Lord promises to restore what the locusts destroyed. No loss is beyond His power to make up.

question.prompt: What lost years might the Lord be able to restore, and how?
exampleAnswers: Time away from the Church, turned into compassion for others who leave.
Years of struggle that became wisdom I can share.

sections.title: I Will Pour Out My Spirit

verses.t: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:
And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: Peter quoted this promise on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:16–18), and the angel Moroni quoted it to Joseph Smith, saying it was about to be fulfilled. The Lord's Spirit is promised to **all flesh**: young and old, men and women.

cards.prompt: How have you seen the Spirit poured out on people you might not have expected: the young, the new, the quiet?
exampleAnswers: A child's simple testimony that moved a whole room.
A new member who taught me something about prayer.
A quiet person's comment that answered my question.
cards.facilitation: This is a good place to invite someone who hasn't spoken yet, gently and only if they seem willing.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: Hosea and Joel show the same Lord: grieved by our wandering, but **never done reaching for us**. Turn to Him, and He will heal, restore, and pour out His Spirit.

youth.title: He never stops reaching
youth.coverMessage: God keeps loving me when I mess up, and He wants my heart, not just my outward show.
youth.background: Hosea was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel about 750 years before Christ. The people had started worshiping idols and trusting other nations instead of God. The Lord asked Hosea to show God's love in a very personal way: when Hosea's wife broke her promises and left, he went and brought her home. Joel, another prophet, saw a huge swarm of locusts wipe out the crops and used it to call people back to God, with a promise that God would restore what was lost.

cards.prompt: What does it feel like when someone forgives you even though you know you let them down?
exampleAnswers: Relief, like I can breathe again.
Kind of embarrassing, but good.
It makes me want to do better for them.

alternates.label: Option B · lighter
alternates.prompt: Who's someone (or a pet) who's always happy to see you, no matter what kind of day you had?
exampleAnswers: My dog.
My grandma.
My little brother, most of the time.

cards.facilitation: Keep it light to start. One or two answers is plenty before you move into the scriptures.

cards.heading: The story
cards.body: Hosea's wife broke her promises and left him. The Lord told Hosea to **go get her and bring her home**, and he did, even paying a price to do it. It was a picture of how God feels about His people when they wander.

verses.t: I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.

cards.prompt: “I will love them freely” means without making them earn it. Why is that hard for us to believe about God?
exampleAnswers: Most love we see has conditions.
We feel like we have to be good enough first.
When we mess up, it's easy to think He's done with us.

alternates.label: Option B · deeper
alternates.prompt: If God's love doesn't have to be earned, why does what we do still matter?
exampleAnswers: Because sin hurts us and the people we love.
Because love wants a relationship, not just forgiveness.
Because coming back is how we feel His love again.

cards.facilitation: If someone says they feel too far gone, don't argue. Point them back to the verse and let it speak.

backups.teaser: God pulls us close with love, not force

verses.t: I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws, and I laid meat unto them.

backups.meaning: God compares Himself to a kind farmer who loosens a heavy yoke and feeds his animals. He draws His people with love.

question.prompt: What kinds of things does God use to draw you closer?
exampleAnswers: People who are kind to me.
Feeling peace when I pray.

verses.t: Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning:
And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.

cards.prompt: Back then, people tore their clothes to show they were sorry. What are ways people today can look sorry without actually changing?
exampleAnswers: Saying sorry just to get out of trouble.
Posting something nice but acting the same.
Feeling bad for a day and then forgetting about it.
cards.facilitation: Keep it about ourselves, not about calling out friends. If examples get pointed, gently redirect.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Show a fancy gift bag that's empty next to a plain paper bag with something real inside. Ask which one is the better gift. God cares about what's inside: a heart that actually turns to Him.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: God isn't impressed by a show. He's **gracious and merciful**, and He's waiting for real hearts to turn to Him.

sections.title: Your Young Men Shall See Visions

verses.t: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

cards.prompt: Joel says the Spirit is for sons and daughters, young and old. How can you tell when the Spirit is talking to you?
exampleAnswers: I feel calm and sure about something.
A thought comes to help someone.
A verse suddenly makes sense.
cards.facilitation: Share a simple experience of your own first. Make it clear there's no single right way to feel the Spirit.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: God never stops reaching for you. **Come back with your whole heart**, and He will heal you and pour out His Spirit on you, too.

cards.title: Where Can I Turn for Peace?

backups.teaser: Getting back what was lost

verses.t: And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.

backups.meaning: After locusts destroyed the crops, God promised to restore the years they had eaten. He can make up for what we've lost.

question.prompt: What's something you feel you've lost that God could help restore?
exampleAnswers: A friendship I messed up.
Confidence after a hard year.

primary.title: Heavenly Father Loves Me Always
primary.coverMessage: When I make mistakes, I can say sorry, and Heavenly Father still loves me.
primary.background: The prophet Hosea taught that even when people turned away from God, He still loved them and wanted them to come back. Through Hosea, the Lord promised to heal them and love them freely (Hosea 14:4).

cards.body: A long time ago, many people stopped listening to Heavenly Father. They made wrong choices. But Heavenly Father didn't stop loving them. He sent a prophet named **Hosea** to tell them to come back. Heavenly Father said: _“I will love them freely.”_ That means He loves us all the time, even when we make mistakes, and He helps us when we say sorry and try again.

cards.title: Coming back
steps: Have one child walk a few steps away from the group, then turn around and walk back while everyone smiles and waves.
Ask: How does it feel when someone is happy to see you come back?
Teach: When we say sorry to Heavenly Father, He is happy we came back to Him.

cards.title: Loved always
cards.scene: A child running back toward open, welcoming arms in a sunny meadow, with flowers growing along the path; no text.

cards.body: Share, simply, that Heavenly Father always loves each child, and that saying sorry helps us feel close to Him again.

reflections: Where is the Lord asking me to go that I've been quietly heading the other way from?
How am I listening for His word through living prophets, and what have I done with what I heard?
Is there someone I've decided doesn't deserve God's mercy? What would Jonah 4 say to me?

adults.title: Prophets, Running, and Mercy
adults.coverMessage: The Lord speaks through His prophets, gives second chances, and extends mercy wider than I might.
adults.background: Amos, a shepherd and fig farmer from Tekoa in Judah, was called to preach in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II, around 760 B.C. (Amos 1:1; 7:14–15). It was a prosperous time, but the wealthy oppressed the poor while keeping up the outward forms of worship. Obadiah is a one-chapter prophecy against Edom, the descendants of Esau, who rejoiced when Jerusalem fell. Jonah was a prophet in the same era as Amos (2 Kings 14:25), sent to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, the empire Israel feared most.

cards.prompt: Is it harder to forgive someone who hurt you, or to watch someone else forgive them? Why?
exampleAnswers: Watching, because it can feel like they got off easy.
Forgiving, because it costs me something.
Both, if part of me still wants them to pay.
cards.facilitation: Let the class sit with the tension; there's no right answer. Jonah felt it too, and ran from mercy he didn't want to give.

verses.t: Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: Amos teaches a pattern: the Lord **reveals His purposes to His servants the prophets** before He acts. Latter-day Saints treasure this verse as a witness that God continues to call living prophets.

cards.prompt: Why would a loving God choose to work through prophets instead of speaking to everyone directly?
exampleAnswers: It invites us to exercise faith and seek our own witness.
It gives one clear, authorized voice for the whole Church.
Prophets can warn us before we see the danger ourselves.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: When has counsel from a prophet blessed you before you understood why it mattered?
exampleAnswers: Counsel to get out of debt, before a job loss.
An invitation to study at home, before our schedule fell apart.
Counsel about ministering that helped me reach a friend.

cards.facilitation: Welcome honest questions. If someone shares a struggle with prophetic counsel, thank them and keep the focus on seeking personal revelation.

backups.teaser: A famine of hearing the word of the Lord

verses.t: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east, they shall run to and fro to seek the word of the LORD, and shall not find it.

backups.meaning: Amos warns of a famine worse than hunger: a time when people would search everywhere for the word of the Lord and not find it. Prophets matter because their absence is a real loss.

question.prompt: How would life feel different without living prophets?
exampleAnswers: We'd have no clear voice when new questions come up.
We'd be left guessing what the Lord wants for our day.

sections.title: Seek Good, That Ye May Live

verses.t: Seek good, and not evil, that ye may live: and so the LORD, the God of hosts, shall be with you, as ye have spoken.
Hate the evil, and love the good, and establish judgment in the gate: it may be that the LORD God of hosts will be gracious unto the remnant of Joseph.

cards.prompt: Amos spoke to a people who went to worship but treated the poor unjustly. What does seeking good look like outside the chapel?
exampleAnswers: Treating employees or coworkers fairly.
Noticing who is struggling in our own neighborhood.
Keeping our word in business and at home.
cards.facilitation: Steer away from political debate. Keep the conversation on what each of us can do personally.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: Worship and how we treat people belong together. The Lord asks us to **“prepare to meet thy God”** (Amos 4:12) by loving good and establishing justice in our own corner of the world.

backups.teaser: A sober call to “prepare to meet thy God”

verses.t: Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.

backups.meaning: After listing warnings Israel ignored, the Lord calls them to prepare to meet Him. It's a solemn invitation to stop putting off repentance.

question.prompt: What does preparing to meet God look like in an ordinary week?
exampleAnswers: Repenting today instead of someday.
Living as though He could walk in at any moment.

cards.heading: The setting
cards.body: Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, a brutal empire and Israel's enemy. When the Lord sent Jonah to call it to repentance, Jonah **boarded a ship going the opposite direction**, to Tarshish.

verses.t: But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly,
And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice.

cards.prompt: Jonah ran, and then prayed from the belly of the fish. What does his story teach about how the Lord responds when we turn back?
exampleAnswers: He hears us even from the depths we put ourselves in.
Running doesn't end His calling for us.
He gives us another chance to do what He asked.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: What are some of the “Tarshishes” we sail toward when the Lord asks something hard?
exampleAnswers: Staying busy so we don't have to think about it.
Telling ourselves someone else will do it.
Waiting for a better time that never comes.

cards.facilitation: Share a light example of your own avoidance first. It makes it safe for others to be honest.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Open a map app and show what happens when you take a wrong turn: it says “rerouting” and finds a new way. The Lord didn't give up on Jonah. He rerouted him, and the word came to Jonah “the second time” (Jonah 3:1).

backups.teaser: Nineveh changes, and God spares the city

verses.t: And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.

backups.meaning: When the people of Nineveh turned from evil, the Lord withheld the destruction He had warned of. His warnings are invitations to change.

question.prompt: What does Nineveh's story teach about how God responds to sincere repentance?
exampleAnswers: He's eager to forgive, even people we'd call enemies.
It's never too late to turn around.

verses.t: Then said the LORD, Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night:
And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?

cards.prompt: Jonah was angry that God forgave his enemies. Why is it sometimes harder to accept God's mercy for others than for ourselves?
exampleAnswers: We want people who hurt us to face consequences.
We think we understand their hearts better than God does.
Mercy for them can feel like it erases our pain.
cards.facilitation: This can touch real hurt. Acknowledge that forgiving is hard, and that God's mercy for others doesn't dismiss our pain.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: The book of Jonah ends with God's question, and no answer from Jonah. The question is left for us: will we rejoice in a God who is **“gracious… and of great kindness”** (Jonah 4:2) to everyone, including people we'd rather He didn't spare?

cards.title: We Thank Thee, O God, for a Prophet

backups.teaser: Saviours on Mount Zion, a hope Latter-day Saints treasure

verses.t: And saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

backups.meaning: Obadiah closes with deliverers on Mount Zion and the kingdom belonging to the Lord. Latter-day Saints often apply the phrase to temple and family history work.

question.prompt: What are small ways we can help bring others to the Lord, living or dead?
exampleAnswers: Finding an ancestor's name and taking it to the temple.
Ministering to someone who's struggling.

backups.teaser: Mercy through temple and family history work
backups.prompt: Latter-day Saints often connect “saviours… upon mount Zion” with temple and family history work. How does serving ancestors reflect the mercy Jonah struggled with?
exampleAnswers: We offer blessings to people we never met and can't judge.
It's mercy that reaches across generations.
We become helpers in someone else's salvation.

youth.title: Running from God (and coming back)
youth.coverMessage: God gives me second chances, and He wants His mercy to reach everyone, even people I don't like.
youth.background: About 760 years before Christ, the Lord called a shepherd named Amos to warn Israel, which was rich but treating poor people badly. Around the same time, the Lord told a prophet named Jonah to go to Nineveh, the capital city of Assyria. Assyria was Israel's scariest enemy, known for its cruelty. Jonah didn't want to go, so he got on a ship headed the opposite way. Obadiah, a short one-chapter book, is a warning to the nation of Edom.

cards.prompt: What's something you knew you should do, but you put off as long as you possibly could?
exampleAnswers: Apologizing to my sister.
Starting a big school project.
Talking to my parents about something.
cards.facilitation: Go first with a funny, low-stakes example to set the tone.

verses.t: But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.

cards.heading: What happened next
cards.body: A huge storm hit the ship. Jonah told the sailors it was his fault, and they threw him overboard. A great fish swallowed him, and **inside the fish, Jonah finally prayed**.

verses.t: Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly,
And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice.

cards.prompt: Jonah ran as far as he could and God still heard him. What does that tell you about praying after you've messed up?
exampleAnswers: It's never too late to pray.
God doesn't wait for you to fix everything first.
Even when you feel far away, He's listening.

alternates.label: Option B · deeper
alternates.prompt: Why do you think Jonah ran instead of just telling God he didn't want to go?
exampleAnswers: He was scared of Nineveh.
He didn't want his enemies to be forgiven.
Avoiding felt easier than an honest conversation.

cards.facilitation: Let the youth notice that Jonah's prayer came at his lowest point. Don't rush past that.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Show a map app and make a wrong turn. Instead of giving up, it says “rerouting.” God did that for Jonah, and He does it for us.

verses.t: And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time, saying,
And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.

cards.prompt: God gave Jonah a second chance, and then gave Nineveh one too. Who might need a second chance from you?
exampleAnswers: A friend who said something mean.
A sibling who keeps bugging me.
Maybe me. I need to give myself one.
cards.facilitation: Invite them to think of a name privately. Nobody needs to say who out loud.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: Jonah was upset that God forgave Nineveh. But God's mercy is **bigger than our grudges**, and He wants it to reach everyone, including us.

backups.teaser: Why Jonah really ran

verses.t: And he prayed unto the LORD, and said, I pray thee, O LORD, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil.

backups.meaning: Jonah admits he fled because he knew God was merciful and would forgive Nineveh. He didn't want his enemies to get a second chance.

question.prompt: Why can it be hard to want good things for people we don't like?
exampleAnswers: It feels unfair if they don't get what they deserve.
Sometimes we want to be right more than we want them to change.

verses.t: Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.

cards.prompt: Amos says God reveals His plans to prophets. Why is it a blessing to have a living prophet today?
exampleAnswers: We get counsel for our time, not just old stories.
It helps us know what matters most when the world is confusing.
We can pray to know it's true for ourselves.
cards.facilitation: If someone mentions recent counsel from the prophet, ask what they did with it. Keep it encouraging.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: God speaks through prophets, hears us even when we run, and **always offers a second chance**. When He asks you to go somewhere hard, you don't have to learn the hard way like Jonah.

cards.title: Come, Listen to a Prophet's Voice

backups.teaser: A famine of hearing God's word

verses.t: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:

backups.meaning: Amos warned of a time when people would be hungry, not for food, but for God's word, and wouldn't be able to find it.

question.prompt: How is having a living prophet like having food on the table?
exampleAnswers: We get what we need when we need it.
You don't notice how much you need it until it's gone.

primary.title: Jonah Learned to Obey
primary.coverMessage: I can listen and obey when Heavenly Father asks me to do something.
primary.background: Jonah was a prophet. When the Lord asked him to go to the city of Nineveh, he got on a ship going the other way. After a storm and a big fish, Jonah obeyed, and the people of Nineveh changed their hearts (Jonah 1–3).

cards.body: Heavenly Father asked **Jonah** to go to a big city called Nineveh and help the people choose the right. But Jonah didn't want to go! He got on a boat going the other way. A big storm came, and Jonah ended up inside a great big fish. In the fish, Jonah prayed. Then _“the LORD spake unto the fish”_ and it put Jonah on dry land. This time, Jonah obeyed and went to Nineveh.

cards.title: Turn around!
