steps: Play “Jonah says”: give simple actions (touch your nose, hop once). When you say “turn around,” everyone turns and walks the other way.
Ask: What did Jonah do when Heavenly Father asked him to go to Nineveh? What did he do the second time?
Teach: When we make a wrong choice, we can turn around and obey.

cards.title: Jonah and the great fish
cards.scene: A large, friendly fish in gentle ocean waves with Jonah stepping out onto a sandy shore under a bright sky; no text.

cards.body: Share, simply, that obeying Heavenly Father brings happiness, and that He gives us another chance when we make mistakes.

reflections: Which of the three, to “do justly,” to “love mercy,” or to “walk humbly with thy God,” needs the most attention in my life right now?
What sins am I still carrying that the Lord has offered to cast “into the depths of the sea”?
Like Habakkuk, what honest question do I need to bring to the Lord, and can I still say “yet I will rejoice”?

adults.title: What Doth the Lord Require?
adults.coverMessage: The Lord asks for justice, mercy and humility, and He delights in mercy toward me.
adults.background: Micah, from the small town of Moresheth, prophesied in Judah in the late 700s B.C., during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Micah 1:1), the same era as Isaiah. Assyria had conquered the northern kingdom and threatened Judah. Nahum, about a century later, foretold the fall of Nineveh, which happened in 612 B.C. Habakkuk wrestled honestly with why the Lord would use the Babylonians to punish Judah in the late 600s B.C. Zephaniah prophesied in the days of King Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1), warning of the day of the Lord and promising joy to a humble remnant.

cards.prompt: If someone asked what God really expects of a person, how would you answer in one sentence?
exampleAnswers: Love Him and love the people around you.
Do your best, and keep coming back when you fall short.
Be honest, be kind, and stay close to Him.
cards.facilitation: Write a few answers on the board. Later in the lesson Micah gives his own one-sentence answer, and you can compare.

cards.heading: The setting
cards.body: Micah imagines someone asking how to please God. Thousands of rams? Rivers of oil? Even a firstborn child? The answer cuts through all of it: the Lord wants **who we are**, not more offerings.

verses.t: Wherewith shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old?
Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

cards.prompt: Why do you think the Lord's answer is three ways of living rather than one more thing to offer?
exampleAnswers: Offerings can be done without changing; these require a changed life.
Justice, mercy and humility show up in every relationship.
He wants our hearts, and these come from the heart.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: Which of the three, do justly, love mercy, or walk humbly, comes easiest to you, and which is hardest?
exampleAnswers: Justice is easy for me; mercy is hard when I've been wronged.
I love mercy, but I don't always walk humbly.
Walking humbly is hardest when I think I'm right.

alternates.label: Option C · deeper
alternates.prompt: How do justice and mercy work together instead of competing?
exampleAnswers: Justice keeps mercy honest; mercy keeps justice kind.
In Christ, both are fully satisfied.
We can hold people accountable and still forgive.

cards.facilitation: Write the three phrases on the board and let the class add examples under each one. It keeps the discussion concrete.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: The Lord doesn't want our religion to be a transaction. He asks us to **do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly** with Him, every day and with everyone.

verses.t: But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: Centuries later, when wise men asked where the King of the Jews would be born, the chief priests pointed to this verse (Matthew 2:5–6). The ruler of Israel would come from **little Bethlehem**, and His “goings forth” were from everlasting.

cards.prompt: Why might it matter that the Savior came from a place described as “little among the thousands of Judah”?
exampleAnswers: God often works through small and humble things.
No one is too ordinary for Him to work through.
It shows the Messiah came to serve, not to impress.
cards.facilitation: If time is short, take one answer and move on. This section sets up the Christmas lessons coming soon.

backups.teaser: Nations streaming to the Lord's house to learn

verses.t: And many nations shall come, and say, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for the law shall go forth of Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.

backups.meaning: Micah sees people from many nations coming to the Lord's house so He can teach them His ways. The temple is pictured as a place of learning that leads to walking in His paths.

question.prompt: What have you learned in the Lord's house that changed how you live?
exampleAnswers: Patience, from seeing things with eternity in view.
That my family's story matters to Him.

verses.t: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.
He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Drop a small pebble into a tall, opaque pitcher of water. It's gone from sight, and you can't easily fish it back out. Micah says the Lord casts our sins “into the depths of the sea.” When He forgives, He doesn't keep them on the shelf to bring out later.

cards.prompt: Micah says the Lord “delighteth in mercy.” How might believing that change the way we approach repentance?
exampleAnswers: We'd come to Him sooner instead of hiding.
Repentance would feel like coming home, not facing a judge.
We'd stop digging up sins He has already forgiven.
cards.facilitation: Pause after the reading. Some may need a moment with the idea that God enjoys forgiving.

cards.heading: The setting
cards.body: Habakkuk opens with a complaint: **“O Lord, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!”** (Habakkuk 1:2). He sees violence and injustice and asks God why. The Lord answers, and Habakkuk ends his book with a song of trust.

verses.t: Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.

cards.prompt: Habakkuk brought his honest questions to God and ended up rejoicing even with empty fields. What helps us move from “how long?” to “yet I will rejoice”?
exampleAnswers: Bringing the question to God instead of away from Him.
Remembering what He has already done.
Finding joy in Him, not in our circumstances.
cards.facilitation: Let it be okay that some people are still in the “how long” part. Rejoicing in the Lord doesn't require pretending things are fine.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: The Lord requires justice, mercy and humility, and He **delights in mercy** toward us. Even when the fields are empty, we can rejoice in the God of our salvation.

backups.teaser: The just shall live by faith

verses.t: Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.

backups.meaning: Habakkuk was told that while the proud are not upright, the righteous will live by their faithfulness, trusting God even before His answers come.

question.prompt: What does living by faith look like while you're still waiting for answers?
exampleAnswers: Keeping my covenants even when I don't understand.
Doing the next right thing without seeing the end.

backups.teaser: The Lord as a stronghold in trouble

verses.t: The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.

backups.meaning: In a book mostly about Nineveh's fall, Nahum pauses to describe the Lord as good, a refuge in hard times, who knows those who trust Him.

question.prompt: What does it mean to you that the Lord knows those who trust Him?
exampleAnswers: I'm not lost in the crowd.
Even small trust is noticed.

backups.teaser: The Lord rejoicing over you with singing

verses.t: The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.

backups.meaning: Zephaniah pictures the Lord in the midst of His people, so delighted with them that He rejoices over them with singing.

question.prompt: How might picturing the Lord rejoicing over you change how you come to Him?
exampleAnswers: With more confidence and less fear.
Remembering He's glad every time I come back.

youth.title: What does God really want?
youth.coverMessage: God wants me to be fair, kind and humble, and He rejoices over me.
youth.background: These four short books come from prophets who lived between about 750 and 600 years before Christ. Micah lived at the same time as Isaiah and warned people that showing up to worship wasn't enough if they treated others unfairly. Nahum promised that the cruel city of Nineveh would fall. Habakkuk asked God some really honest questions about why bad things were happening. Zephaniah promised that God would rejoice over His people.

cards.prompt: If you had to sum up what it means to be a good person in just three words, what would they be?
exampleAnswers: Kind, honest, loyal.
Fair, forgiving, humble.
Show up, help out, listen.
cards.facilitation: Collect a few answers on the board. You'll compare them with Micah's three in a minute.

verses.t: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

cards.prompt: What would doing justly, loving mercy, and walking humbly look like at school this week?
exampleAnswers: Not cheating, even when everyone else is.
Giving someone a break when they mess up.
Not acting like I'm better than other people.

alternates.label: Option B · deeper
alternates.prompt: Why do you think God puts “walk humbly with thy God” right next to how we treat people?
exampleAnswers: Being close to God makes us kinder.
Pride ruins both kinds of relationships.
It's hard to be fair and merciful if we think we're better.

cards.facilitation: Compare their opening words with Micah's. Notice how much overlap there is, and let them feel that they already understand what God wants.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Show a three-legged stool, or set a book on three stacked cups. Take one leg away and it tips over. Justice, mercy and humility work the same way: we need all three.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: God isn't looking for a show. He wants us to be **fair, kind, and humble**, and He'll help us become that.

backups.teaser: Sins cast into the depths of the sea

verses.t: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.
He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

backups.meaning: Micah marvels at a God who delights in mercy and promises to throw His people's sins into the deepest part of the sea.

question.prompt: Why is the bottom of the sea a good picture of what God does with forgiven sins?
exampleAnswers: Once they sink, you can't get them back.
They're gone for good, not just hidden.

verses.t: O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: Habakkuk was a prophet, and he still asked God, “How long?” God didn't scold him. He answered, and by the end Habakkuk was singing that he would **rejoice in the Lord** even if everything went wrong.

verses.t: Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.

cards.prompt: Is it okay to ask God hard questions? What does Habakkuk show you?
exampleAnswers: Yes. A prophet did it, and God answered.
Asking God is better than giving up on Him.
Questions can lead to stronger faith.
cards.facilitation: Make clear that questions are welcome in your class too. If someone asks a hard one, it's fine to say “let's look for that together.”

verses.t: The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.

cards.prompt: Zephaniah says God will rejoice over you with singing. How does it feel to think God is happy about you?
exampleAnswers: Hard to believe, honestly.
It makes me want to do better.
Like being loved without having to prove anything.
cards.facilitation: Some youth may struggle to believe this about themselves. Let the verse do the work, and add your own testimony if it feels right.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: God asks you to be fair, kind and humble, listens to your hardest questions, and **rejoices over you**. That's what He really wants.

backups.teaser: God is a safe place when things are hard

verses.t: The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.

backups.meaning: Nahum says the Lord is good, a stronghold when trouble comes, and that He knows those who trust Him.

question.prompt: Where do you go when things get hard, and how could God be part of that?
exampleAnswers: My room, and I could pray there.
Music, and I could choose songs that bring the Spirit.

primary.title: Be Kind and Fair
primary.coverMessage: Heavenly Father wants me to be fair, kind and humble.
primary.background: The prophet Micah taught that what Heavenly Father wants most is for His children to be fair, to be kind, and to stay close to Him (Micah 6:8).

cards.body: Long ago, some people wondered what gift they could give Heavenly Father. Maybe lots of animals? Maybe lots of oil? A prophet named **Micah** told them what Heavenly Father really wants: _“to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.”_ That means: be fair, be kind, and stay close to Heavenly Father. That is the best gift we can give Him!

cards.title: Three kind steps
steps: Hold up three fingers and name one with each: be fair, be kind, stay close to Heavenly Father.
Act out short situations (sharing a toy, taking turns, helping someone who fell) and let the children show the kind choice.
Teach: Every kind choice is a gift to Heavenly Father.

cards.title: Kind hands
cards.scene: Children sharing a toy, helping a friend up from the ground, and holding hands in a circle under a big tree; no text.

cards.body: Share, simply, that being kind and fair makes Heavenly Father happy, and that He helps us be kind.

reflections: When the Lord says “consider your ways,” what have I been building for myself while His work waits?
Where am I trying to succeed by my own might instead of “by my spirit,” as the Lord said?
What ordinary part of my life could I treat as “HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD” this week?

adults.title: Holiness unto the Lord
adults.coverMessage: When I put the Lord first, He makes my efforts enough, and He wants holiness written on all of my life.
adults.background: In about 538 B.C., Cyrus of Persia allowed exiles from Judah to return home and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. They laid the foundation, then stopped for years amid opposition and their own busy lives. In 520 B.C. the prophets Haggai and Zechariah urged the governor Zerubbabel, the high priest Joshua, and the people to finish the Lord's house (Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 1:1). The temple was completed around 515 B.C. Zechariah's visions also look far ahead, to the Messiah and to a day when holiness marks everything.

cards.prompt: What's a project you started with real excitement and then let stall? What got in the way?
exampleAnswers: A garden I planted and then ignored all summer.
Family history: life just got busy.
A habit like daily prayer that slipped during a hard year.
cards.facilitation: Keep it light and honest. The people in this week's reading started rebuilding something important, then stopped for years.

cards.heading: The setting
cards.body: The returned exiles had built comfortable, paneled homes, while the temple foundation sat unfinished. They worked hard, yet never seemed to have enough. Haggai asked them to **consider their ways**.

verses.t: Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your ceiled houses, and this house lie waste?
Now therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways.

Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.

cards.prompt: Haggai describes earning wages only to put them “into a bag with holes.” What does it feel like to work hard on the wrong priorities?
exampleAnswers: Busy but never satisfied.
Always behind, no matter how much I do.
Like my effort leaks away before it matters.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: What “temple” in your life, something sacred, has been waiting while other things got built first?
exampleAnswers: Temple attendance that kept getting pushed back.
Family scripture study we always meant to start.
A calling I've been doing halfway.

cards.facilitation: Keep this reflective rather than guilt-inducing. Invite quiet personal answers before asking anyone to share.

backups.teaser: Be strong and work, for the Lord is with you

verses.t: Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, saith the LORD; and be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest; and be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you, saith the LORD of hosts:

backups.meaning: When the builders felt their temple would never match the old one, the Lord told the leaders and the people to be strong and keep working, because He was with them.

question.prompt: When has knowing the Lord was with you given you strength to keep going?
exampleAnswers: In a calling that felt bigger than me.
Raising kids through a hard season.

sections.title: Not by Might, nor by Power

verses.t: Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.

cards.prompt: Zerubbabel faced a huge task with limited resources. Why might the Lord want His work done “by my spirit” rather than by might or power?
exampleAnswers: So we know the success is His, not ours.
Because the Spirit can do what resources can't.
It invites ordinary people to take part.
cards.facilitation: If someone shares a time they felt inadequate in a calling, thank them. It's a good bridge to how the Lord magnifies small efforts.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: The Lord's work isn't finished by the strongest or best funded. It's finished **by His Spirit**, working through people willing to keep building.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: In Zechariah's vision, Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the Lord in **filthy garments**, a symbol of sin. The Lord commands that they be taken away, and Joshua is clothed in clean, new clothing.

verses.t: Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments, and stood before the angel.

And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Show a muddy work shirt and a clean, folded one. Joshua didn't scrub his own garments clean. They were taken away and replaced. That's what the Savior offers us.

cards.prompt: Joshua didn't clean his own clothes; they were replaced for him. How does that help you understand the Savior's role in repentance?
exampleAnswers: We repent, but He is the one who makes us clean.
We can't scrub away sin by effort alone.
He gives us something new, not just a patched version of the old.
cards.facilitation: Let a few answers come before you add your own testimony of the Savior's power to cleanse.

verses.t: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: Five centuries later, Jesus fulfilled this prophecy when He entered Jerusalem riding on a colt (Matthew 21:4–5). Zechariah also foresaw a day when even the bells on horses would read **“HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD.”**

verses.t: In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD; and the pots in the LORD's house shall be like the bowls before the altar.

cards.prompt: Zechariah pictures holiness written on ordinary things like bells and cooking pots. What would it mean to make the ordinary parts of our week holy?
exampleAnswers: Doing our jobs honestly, as if for the Lord.
Treating meals and family time as sacred.
Remembering Him in small, everyday choices.
cards.facilitation: Invite a few concrete examples. Ordinary answers are exactly the point here.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: Haggai and Zechariah called a discouraged people to **put the Lord's house first**, trust His Spirit, and let Him make them clean. The King they waited for came lowly, and He invites us to write holiness on all of life.

backups.teaser: Wounds received in the house of His friends

verses.t: And one shall say unto him, What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends.

backups.meaning: Zechariah describes someone asked about the wounds in his hands, who answers that he received them among his friends. Latter-day Saints see the Savior here, wounded by His own people.

question.prompt: What does it teach you that the Savior's wounds came from those close to Him?
exampleAnswers: He understands being hurt by people we love.
His love didn't stop even when His own rejected Him.

backups.teaser: Looking on Him whom they pierced

verses.t: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.

backups.meaning: The Lord promises to pour out a spirit of grace and pleading, and His people will look on the one they pierced and mourn. John's Gospel applies this to the Crucifixion (John 19:37).

question.prompt: How can remembering the Savior's suffering soften our hearts?
exampleAnswers: It makes me grateful instead of complacent.
It helps me take repentance seriously.

youth.title: First things first
youth.coverMessage: When I put God first, He makes my efforts enough.
youth.background: About 500 years before Christ, the Jewish people were finally allowed to go home after being exiled in Babylon. They started rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem, but then they stopped and focused on their own houses instead. For years the temple sat unfinished. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah told them to get back to work, and with their encouragement the temple was finished.

cards.prompt: What's something you always mean to get to, but other stuff keeps coming first?
exampleAnswers: Reading my scriptures.
Practicing piano.
Calling my grandparents.
cards.facilitation: Share your own honest answer first. It makes the rest of the lesson feel like a conversation, not a lecture.

verses.t: Now therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways.

Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Poke a few holes in the bottom of a paper cup and pour water in over a bowl. No matter how much you pour, it never stays full. Haggai said life feels like that when we leave God out.

cards.prompt: What are some things that feel like a “bag with holes,” things that take a lot from us but never leave us full?
exampleAnswers: Scrolling for hours.
Trying to make everyone like me.
Buying stuff I don't need.

alternates.label: Option B · deeper
alternates.prompt: Why do you think putting God first makes everything else feel more like enough?
exampleAnswers: He helps us see what actually matters.
Peace comes from Him, not from having more.
When He's first, the rest falls into place better.

cards.facilitation: Avoid lecturing about phones. Let the youth name the holes themselves.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: Haggai's message is simple: **consider your ways**. When we put God first, He helps the rest of our life hold together.

backups.teaser: Be strong and keep working: God is with you

verses.t: Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, saith the LORD; and be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest; and be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you, saith the LORD of hosts:

backups.meaning: When the temple builders felt discouraged, God told them to be strong and keep working, because He was with them.

question.prompt: What's something you're working on that would feel different if you knew God was with you?
exampleAnswers: School, when it gets overwhelming.
Trying to be a better example at home.

verses.t: Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.

cards.prompt: The temple builders didn't have much money or power. How can “by my spirit” help you with something that feels too big for you?
exampleAnswers: I don't have to do it all alone.
God can help me find a way I haven't thought of.
Praying first helps me feel calmer about it.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: What's something hard you're facing right now where you could use God's help more than your own strength?
exampleAnswers: A class I'm failing.
A friendship that's falling apart.
Feeling anxious all the time.

cards.facilitation: Personal answers here may be heavy. Thank anyone who shares, and follow up privately if something concerns you.

verses.t: In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD; and the pots in the LORD's house shall be like the bowls before the altar.

cards.prompt: Zechariah imagined “HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD” written even on horse bells. What everyday thing in your life could you make holy?
exampleAnswers: How I talk to my family.
What I post online.
How I treat people at practice.
cards.facilitation: Encourage one specific, small idea. Small and real beats big and vague.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: Put God first, lean on **His Spirit, not just your strength**, and let holiness show up in the ordinary parts of your life.

backups.teaser: The King arrives, humble on a colt

verses.t: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.

backups.meaning: Zechariah foresaw a king coming to Jerusalem, not on a war horse, but humbly on a young donkey. Jesus fulfilled this when He rode into Jerusalem.

question.prompt: Why do you think the Savior chose to come humbly instead of with power?
exampleAnswers: To show His kingdom is different.
So anyone would feel they could come to Him.

primary.title: Building the Temple
primary.coverMessage: The temple is Heavenly Father's house, and I can get ready to go there.
primary.background: After the people came home from a faraway land, they started building the temple again, then stopped. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged them to be strong and finish it, and the Lord promised to be with them (Haggai 1–2).

cards.title: I Love to See the Temple

cards.body: A long time ago, the people started building a temple, Heavenly Father's house. But they got busy with their own houses and stopped. The prophet **Haggai** told them to keep building. Heavenly Father told them to be strong _“and work: for I am with you.”_ So the people worked together and finished the beautiful temple.

cards.title: Build a temple together
steps: Give each child a block, cup or folded card to add to a “temple” the class builds together.
As each piece is added, ask the child to name one way to get ready for the temple (be kind, pray, obey).
Teach: We each help build Heavenly Father's kingdom, and He is with us.

cards.title: Heavenly Father's house
cards.scene: A simple temple with a tall spire under a bright sky, with families walking toward it on a garden path; no text.

cards.body: Share, simply, that the temple is a holy place and that each child can prepare now to go there one day.

reflections: When the Lord says “Return unto me, and I will return unto you,” what is one step back toward Him I can take this week?
How have I seen the Lord “open… the windows of heaven” in my life, sometimes in ways I didn't expect?
Whose heart, among my ancestors or my family now, could I turn toward this week?

adults.title: Return unto Me
adults.coverMessage: The Lord has loved me all along, and when I return to Him, He returns to me.
adults.background: Malachi, whose name means “my messenger,” is the last book of the Old Testament. It likely comes from the mid-400s B.C., about a century after the temple was rebuilt, in the era of Ezra and Nehemiah. The excitement of the return from exile had faded. Priests offered blemished animals, people held back their tithes, and many wondered aloud whether serving God made any difference. Malachi answers with the Lord's love, His call to return, and a promise that Elijah would come before the great day of the Lord.

cards.prompt: How can you tell when you've drifted from someone, even if nothing dramatic happened?
exampleAnswers: Our conversations stay on the surface.
I stop thinking to call them.
Reaching out starts to feel awkward.
cards.facilitation: Keep this about relationships in general. Malachi spoke to people who hadn't rebelled so much as slowly cooled.

verses.t: I have loved you, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us? Was not Esau Jacob's brother? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob,

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: The Lord opens with love, and the people answer, “Wherein hast thou loved us?” Malachi is written as a **conversation**: the Lord speaks, the people push back, and the Lord answers their doubts one by one.

cards.prompt: Why might people who have seen so much of God's help still ask, “Wherein hast thou loved us?”
exampleAnswers: Hard times make it easy to forget past blessings.
When life is routine, God's hand is harder to notice.
Disappointment can turn into doubt.
cards.facilitation: Make room for honesty. Most of us have asked a version of this question at some point.

backups.teaser: A book of remembrance for those who fear the Lord

verses.t: Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him.

backups.meaning: While others complained, the faithful talked together about the Lord, and He listened and had their names recorded. He calls them His own treasure.

question.prompt: What does it mean to you that the Lord notices when believers simply talk together about Him?
exampleAnswers: Our quiet conversations matter to Him.
Faith shared among friends is remembered in heaven.

verses.t: Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. But ye said, Wherein shall we return?
Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.
Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation.

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.

cards.prompt: Right after inviting the people to return, the Lord talks about tithes and offerings. How can tithing be a way of returning to Him?
exampleAnswers: It puts Him first in a concrete, measurable way.
It's an act of trust in His promises.
Giving back reminds us everything came from Him.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: How have you seen the windows of heaven opened, perhaps in ways other than money?
exampleAnswers: We somehow always had enough, even in a tight year.
Peace about our finances that I can't explain.
Opportunities that came at just the right time.

alternates.label: Option C · deeper
alternates.prompt: The Lord says, “Return unto me, and I will return unto you.” What does that teach about how a relationship with Him works?
exampleAnswers: He respects our agency and waits for us to turn.
Every step we take toward Him, He meets.
The distance was on our side, not His.

cards.facilitation: Tithing can be a sensitive subject, especially for those struggling financially. Keep the focus on trust and blessings, and avoid any comment that could feel like judgment.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: The Lord never moved away from Israel. **“Return unto me, and I will return unto you”** is an invitation to anyone who has drifted, and tithing is one way of showing Him we're coming back.

verses.t: But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:
And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Show a tarnished silver spoon or piece of jewelry, then polish part of it with a cloth. A refiner works patiently until the metal is pure and reflects light. The Lord refines us the same way: carefully, and with a purpose.

cards.prompt: A refiner “shall sit” and watch the silver closely. How might it change our trials to know the Lord is attentive during the refining?
exampleAnswers: We aren't left alone in the heat.
The process has a purpose and an end.
He knows exactly how much we can bear.
cards.facilitation: Be careful not to suggest that every hardship is sent by God. Keep the focus on how He is present and purposeful in our growth.

backups.teaser: A messenger to prepare the Lord's way

verses.t: Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts.

backups.meaning: The Lord promises to send a messenger to prepare His way, and then to come suddenly to His temple. The New Testament identifies John the Baptist as that messenger (Matthew 11:10).

question.prompt: How does the Lord prepare people today before He works in their lives?
exampleAnswers: Through someone who speaks up at the right moment.
Through experiences that make us ready to listen.

verses.t: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD:
And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse.

cards.heading: What this means
cards.body: The angel Moroni quoted this promise to Joseph Smith in 1823, with some differences in wording. On April 3, 1836, Elijah appeared in the Kirtland Temple and restored the **sealing power**, which binds families together on earth and in heaven (Doctrine and Covenants 110:13–16).

cards.prompt: What does it look like to have our hearts turned to our ancestors, and to our children?
exampleAnswers: Learning the stories of the people we come from.
Taking family names to the temple.
Passing faith and family history on to our kids.
cards.facilitation: Family can be a painful topic for some. Acknowledge that turning hearts can include healing, and that the Lord can help with what we can't fix.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: The Old Testament ends with a promise, not a period. The Lord has loved us all along; He invites us to **return**, refines us with care, and turns hearts across generations through the power Elijah restored.

youth.title: Come back home
youth.coverMessage: God never stopped loving me, and when I turn toward Him, He turns toward me.
youth.background: Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament, written about 400 years before Jesus was born. The temple had been rebuilt, but people were getting lazy about their faith. They gave God their leftovers, skipped paying tithing, and asked whether serving Him even mattered. Through Malachi, God reminded them that He loved them and invited them to come back.

cards.prompt: Have you ever drifted away from a friend without really meaning to? What helped you reconnect?
exampleAnswers: One of us just texted first.
We ended up in the same class again.
I realized I missed them and said so.
cards.facilitation: Keep it light. You're setting up the idea that drifting happens slowly, and so does coming back.

verses.t: Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. But ye said, Wherein shall we return?

cards.prompt: God says, “Return unto me, and I will return unto you.” What's one small way someone your age can turn back toward God?
exampleAnswers: Praying again after not praying for a while.
Coming to church even when I'm not sure.
Talking to a parent or leader about it.

alternates.label: Option B · deeper
alternates.prompt: Who moves first in that verse, us or God? Why does that matter?
exampleAnswers: We take the first step, and He meets us.
He respects our choice to come back.
It means it's never too late to start.

cards.facilitation: Avoid putting anyone on the spot about their own drifting. Invite private thinking first.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: God never left. When we turn back, **He turns toward us**, every time.

backups.teaser: “I have loved you,” and the people's doubt

verses.t: I have loved you, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us? Was not Esau Jacob's brother? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob,

backups.meaning: Malachi opens with God saying He loves His people, and them asking how. God points back to how He has cared for them since Jacob.

question.prompt: Why do people sometimes struggle to feel God's love even when He's shown it?
exampleAnswers: When life gets hard, it's easy to forget.
We look for big signs and miss the small ones.

verses.t: Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Set a cup on a tray and keep pouring water until it overflows. God promises a blessing so big that “there shall not be room enough to receive it.”

cards.prompt: God says, “prove me now herewith,” which basically means try it and see. Why do you think He invites us to test His promise?
exampleAnswers: So we can see for ourselves that He keeps His word.
Trusting Him builds our faith.
He wants us to know Him, not just hear about Him.
cards.facilitation: If youth mention paying tithing on their own money, celebrate it. Don't ask who does or doesn't pay.

verses.t: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD:
And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse.

cards.prompt: Elijah came back to restore the power that seals families together. How can you turn your heart toward your family, past or present, this week?
exampleAnswers: Ask a grandparent about their life.
Find a family name to take to the temple.
Be kinder to my siblings.
cards.facilitation: Some youth have hard family situations. Include ancestors and future family, not only the family they live with now.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: The whole Old Testament ends with a promise: God will **turn hearts toward each other**. He's been turning His heart toward you all along.

primary.title: Families Are Forever
primary.coverMessage: I can learn about my family and help families be together forever.
primary.background: The prophet Malachi said that Elijah would come to turn the hearts of families toward each other (Malachi 4:5–6). Latter-day Saints believe Elijah came to restore the power that seals families together in the temple.

cards.body: The prophet **Malachi** promised that another prophet, **Elijah**, would come back one day. When he came, he would _“turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers.”_ That means helping families love each other and be together forever. When we learn about our grandparents and great-grandparents, our hearts turn toward them too!

cards.title: My family heart
steps: Give each child a paper heart and help them draw or write the names of people in their family.
Invite a child to share one thing they know about a grandparent or someone from long ago.
Teach: Heavenly Father wants families to love each other and be together forever.

cards.title: Hearts turned together
cards.scene: A family of children, parents and grandparents holding hands in a row, with a large heart shape behind them and a temple in the distance; no text.

cards.body: Share, simply, that families can be together forever through Heavenly Father's plan, and that each child is part of a family He loves.

weeks.theme: Unto You Is Born a Saviour
reflections: Which of the Savior's names in Isaiah 9:6 means the most to me this Christmas, and why?
Like the shepherds who “came with haste,” what would it look like for me to hurry toward Christ this week?
Mary “kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.” What from this year do I want to keep and ponder?

adults.title: Unto You Is Born a Saviour
adults.coverMessage: The child Isaiah foretold was born in Bethlehem, and His birth is good tidings of great joy for me.
adults.background: Isaiah wrote chapter 9 in the 730s B.C., when Assyria was overrunning the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali around Galilee. Into that darkness he promised a great light and a child who would reign in peace. Seven centuries later, Luke records the fulfillment: Caesar Augustus ordered a census, Joseph and Mary traveled to Bethlehem, and Jesus was born and laid in a manger. Luke 2 goes on to tell of shepherds, of Simeon and Anna recognizing the child at the temple, and of Jesus at twelve in His Father's house.

cards.prompt: What's a Christmas memory that still means a lot to you, and why?
exampleAnswers: The year we had almost nothing, and someone left gifts on our porch.
Singing carols at a care center with my family.
Reading the Christmas story by candlelight with my parents.
cards.facilitation: Let a few people share, then turn toward the first Christmas and the people who had been waiting for it.

verses.t: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined.

cards.prompt: Isaiah spoke to people in real darkness: war, fear and loss. How has the Savior been a light for you in a dark season?
exampleAnswers: Hope after a loss, when nothing else made sense.
A sense of direction when I didn't know what to do next.
Peace in a Christmas season that was hard for our family.
cards.facilitation: Christmas can be painful for some. Acknowledge that the light came to people sitting in darkness, which means it's for them too.

verses.t: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.

Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will perform this.

cards.prompt: Isaiah gives the child five names: Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. Which one speaks to you right now, and why?
exampleAnswers: Counsellor. I need direction this year.
Prince of Peace. Our home needs peace.
The mighty God. I need to remember He's strong enough for my problem.

alternates.label: Option B · deeper
alternates.prompt: What do these names together teach about who Jesus Christ is and what He came to do?
exampleAnswers: He is both mighty and gentle.
He came to rule, and to rule with peace and justice.
He is divine, not just a great teacher.

cards.facilitation: List the five names on the board and let people come up and mark the one that speaks to them. It invites quieter members in.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: The baby in Bethlehem is the **Mighty God and Prince of Peace** Isaiah foresaw. His government and peace will have no end.

cards.heading: The setting
cards.body: Shepherds were ordinary working people, often looked down on. Yet they were the first to hear the announcement, out in the fields at night, not in a palace or the temple.

verses.t: And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night.
And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid.
And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.
For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Hold up a wrapped gift addressed “To You.” The angel didn't say a Saviour was born to the world in general, but **“unto you.”** Ask: what changes when a gift is addressed to you personally?

cards.prompt: Why do you think the first announcement of the Savior's birth went to shepherds?
exampleAnswers: It shows He came for ordinary and overlooked people.
Shepherds would recognize the Good Shepherd.
God's news doesn't need the approval of the powerful.
cards.facilitation: Let a few people answer, then ask who in our community might feel like the shepherds: overlooked and needing good news.

backups.teaser: Simeon holds the child and praises God

verses.t: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word:
For mine eyes have seen thy salvation,
Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people;
A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.

backups.meaning: The aged Simeon, promised that he would see the Messiah, takes the baby in his arms and says he can now depart in peace, because he has seen the Lord's salvation.

question.prompt: What would it mean to say, like Simeon, “mine eyes have seen thy salvation”?
exampleAnswers: That a long wait was worth it.
That I've recognized Christ in my own life.

backups.teaser: Anna, the aged prophetess who recognized Him

verses.t: And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser: she was of a great age, and had lived with an husband seven years from her virginity;
And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day.
And she coming in that instant gave thanks likewise unto the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem.

backups.meaning: Anna, a widow who had served God in the temple for decades, recognized the child and spoke of Him to everyone waiting for redemption.

question.prompt: What can we learn from Anna about waiting faithfully?
exampleAnswers: Daily devotion prepared her to recognize Him.
Long waiting doesn't mean God has forgotten.

verses.t: But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.

cards.prompt: In a busy season, Mary kept and pondered. What helps you slow down enough to ponder the Savior at Christmas?
exampleAnswers: Reading Luke 2 as a family on Christmas Eve.
Choosing one quiet moment a day without screens.
Serving someone, which turns my thoughts to Him.
cards.facilitation: Invite each person to choose one idea for this week, and offer to share your own.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: The light Isaiah promised has come. **Unto you is born a Saviour**, and like the shepherds we can come with haste, and like Mary we can keep these things in our hearts.

backups.teaser: How Jesus grew: four ways

verses.t: And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.

backups.meaning: Luke sums up Jesus's youth in one verse: He grew in wisdom, in stature, and in favor with God and with people.

question.prompt: Which of these four kinds of growth do you most want to focus on in the new year?
exampleAnswers: Wisdom: I want to study more deeply.
Favor with God: more sincere prayer.

youth.title: Good news for you
youth.coverMessage: Jesus was born for me, and His birth is good news worth hurrying toward.
youth.background: Hundreds of years before Jesus was born, the prophet Isaiah promised that a child would come who would be called the Prince of Peace. Luke tells how it happened: Mary and Joseph traveled to Bethlehem because of a government census, couldn't find a room, and laid the baby Jesus in a manger. Angels told shepherds in the fields, and they hurried to find Him.

cards.prompt: What's a Christmas tradition in your family, and does it have anything to do with Jesus?
exampleAnswers: We read the Christmas story on Christmas Eve.
We set up a nativity scene.
Honestly, mostly presents, but I'd like that to change.
cards.facilitation: Welcome every kind of answer, including fun ones. You're building toward why the real story matters.

verses.t: And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.
For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.

cards.prompt: The angel said, “unto you is born… a Saviour.” What's the difference between Jesus being born for the world and Him being born for you?
exampleAnswers: It makes it personal, not just history.
It means He knows me and came for me.
It changes how I think about my own mistakes.

alternates.label: Option B · personal
alternates.prompt: What part of the Christmas story feels most real or meaningful to you?
exampleAnswers: That there was no room, and Mary and Joseph kept going.
The shepherds, because they were just regular people.
That Jesus started as a baby, small and vulnerable.

cards.facilitation: Leave a little silence after reading. Let the words “unto you” sink in before taking answers.

cards.title: Object lesson
cards.body: Turn off the lights and turn on a single flashlight. One small light changes the whole room. Isaiah promised that people in darkness would see “a great light,” and that light came as a baby in Bethlehem.

cards.heading: Teach
cards.body: The good news isn't just that a Saviour was born. It's that He was born **unto you**.

backups.teaser: Isaiah's names for the promised child

verses.t: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.

backups.meaning: Centuries before Jesus was born, Isaiah gave the promised child five names that describe who He is.

question.prompt: Which of these names would mean the most to you this week, and why?
exampleAnswers: Prince of Peace, because things have felt stressful.
Counsellor, because I need advice.

verses.t: And it came to pass, as the angels were gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds said one to another, Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing which is come to pass, which the Lord hath made known unto us.
And they came with haste, and found Mary, and Joseph, and the babe lying in a manger.
And when they had seen it, they made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child.

cards.prompt: The shepherds didn't wait until morning; they “came with haste.” Then they told everyone. What would hurrying toward Jesus look like for you this Christmas?
exampleAnswers: Reading the Christmas story myself, not just hearing it.
Doing something kind for someone who's lonely.
Praying and actually thanking Him for coming.
cards.facilitation: Encourage one specific idea each. If it fits your class, invite them to report back next week.

verses.t: And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.

cards.prompt: Jesus grew in wisdom, in stature, in favour with God, and with people. Which of those four do you most want to grow in this coming year?
exampleAnswers: Wisdom. I want to make better choices.
With God. I want my prayers to feel real.
With people. I want to be a better friend.
cards.facilitation: This is a good setup for personal goals. Let them think privately first, and share only if they want.

cards.heading: Close
cards.body: Jesus was born for you, and He grew up step by step like you. This Christmas, **come with haste**, and let Him help you grow.

primary.title: Jesus Was Born
primary.coverMessage: Jesus was born in Bethlehem because Heavenly Father loves me.
primary.background: Long before Jesus was born, the prophet Isaiah promised a special child would come (Isaiah 9:6). Luke tells how Jesus was born in Bethlehem, laid in a manger, and visited by shepherds (Luke 2).

cards.body: **Mary** and **Joseph** traveled to a town called Bethlehem. There was no room for them at the inn, so they stayed where the animals slept. That night baby **Jesus** was born. Mary _“wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger.”_ Angels told shepherds the happy news, and the shepherds hurried to see the baby Jesus.

cards.title: Act out the Christmas story
steps: Give simple roles (Mary, Joseph, shepherds, angels, animals) and a blanket or cloth for the baby.
Read or tell the story slowly while the children act it out.
Teach: Jesus was born so He could be our Savior, because Heavenly Father loves us.

cards.title: Baby Jesus in the manger
cards.scene: Mary and Joseph kneeling beside baby Jesus in a manger in a simple stable, with a lamb and a bright star shining above; no text.

cards.body: Share, simply, your love for Jesus Christ and that His birth is the happiest news in the world.
